text: Good evening, Mr. Deputy Mayor, members of the council, Tiffany Speer. I will share a PowerPoint, which is actually also in your packet tonight, starting at page 206. It began earlier this year when there was a resolution adopted that said, we need an ad hoc committee to explain how and define what should be in a Comprehensive Plan to End Homelessness with the idea initially, as reflected in the May 25th resolution they adopted, that by the end of this year, there would be a plan. The City of Lakewood representative, myself, participated in both the initial ad hoc committee and then the committee that was creating the plan throughout the year. Last Tuesday, on December 7th, there was a presentation made to the county's Human Services Committee, which summarized the plan itself. First and foremost, the idea was to provide what is the state of the situation right now? What are the costs or cost benefit actually that might come from a comprehensive effort toward ending homelessness in the county? And then also one of the bigger items that I just wanted to make sure you were aware of as a council is there's a suggestion in the plan that there be created what they're calling a unit, excuse me, a unit, we'll get to it. I've lost it, sorry. There's six goals within the plan. There it is, Unified Homeless System. And the idea under strategy 1.1, it's called a Unified Regional Office of Homelessness. And this is a somewhat different approach than has happened historically, as you know, in the county for homelessness services. There's been non-profits and non-governmental organizations working in this arena. And then jurisdictions have worked independently regarding homelessness, but this is an effort to create something that would be not only for Pierce County, but for the cities within the county to be working together. The idea here is cost-effectiveness and unified performance for the people experiencing homelessness. And so there'd have to be some changes happening on the inside of the system, if you will, where a single organization worked to coordinate efforts, potentially coordinate funding, and potentially be actually a governing organization for all of the different jurisdictions and agencies dealing with homelessness in Pierce County. And so here you'll see coordination among the partners. You'll see those various items listed, including the cities and towns. So again, the idea is to create a new standup organization for a coordinated effort to work to end homelessness. The idea here as well is to track information about those experiencing homelessness in order to be able to, over time, address those issues further and further, quote, upstream, meaning making it easier and easier for someone to stay out of homelessness or a family to stay out of homelessness, because there would be some data where maybe agencies can anticipate those at risk and assist them before they actually end up on the street. As of now, Pierce County Human Services deals with the county's homeless program, but the idea presented to the county council last week was maybe they would hand the reins over to this new unified regional office as well. The second goal in there is to talk about targeted universalism, which is something which is truly trying to look at the population experiencing homelessness from all angles and trying to understand how to best provide the services needed by everyone. So this is regardless of gender, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity, religion, any sort of disability, just making sure that the way the homeless system is run, it is accessible to anyone and everyone. Preventing homelessness was an issue raised and stressed. And historically in the homelessness world, prevention hasn't been a big item. It's been handling the crisis of someone or a family who is on the street right now and how to get them off the street. This plan is talking about, we need to be looking again that upstream term where we're trying to prevent anyone from having to experience homelessness before getting help. Fourth goal is to making easier the coordination among various quote systems. So whether it's the foster system, the criminal justice system, behavioral health, workforce development, all of these different almost siloed systems within our communities, having them talk to each other more often and more consistently to help develop more of a common understanding across the different systems and communication across the different systems, potentially for how to help prevent homelessness for a family, for an individual that may be more than one system is working on or working with without knowing that other systems are as well. So an unfair labor practice complaint is actually a complaint either made by a union or by management to PERC, which is the Public Employment Relationship Commission. And what they do is they basically regulate and moderate the relationship between unions and management. And either side can go to them and make an unfair labor practice complaint, which is referred to as a ULP. In this case, the police union, LPIG, filed their ULP in mid-May of 2019. And there's an interesting story about what was happening at the time. The union was in a state of complete disarray. Jeremy Vallee was the president of the union and he was basically in the process of being recalled by the members. And the results of the recall election were very unclear and uncertain. So this was, it resembled sort of like ancient Rome when one Caesar was trying to get rid of another or perhaps a reality show on Bravo. But there was a lot of disarray going on. Jeremy Vallee actually filed the unfair labor practice complaint. And if you look at the complaint, about 80% of the complaint is directed at his fellow union executive board members and at his fellow union members. There are, at the tail end of his complaint, some allegations against the city. And those are the only things that PERC allowed to proceed to a hearing were four allegations against the city. And I'll briefly summarize those. The first was Chief Zaro asked the guild board if it supported taking a grievance over Sergeant Navasky's demotion to arbitration. And this is based on a contract provision that says that an individual union member can grieve his discipline internally, but in order to take it to arbitration and have an arbitrator decide, the union has to support the grievance. So he was basically asking the executive board, Sergeant Navasky wants to grieve to arbitration his demotion, do you support it? The second claim had to do with a very similar set of circumstances. And that's a few months later, another police officer was fired, Eric Bell, and the city got a request to take that to arbitration. And Chief Zaro asked again, does the union support this grievance and taking it to arbitration? And the reason why Chief Zaro was asking these questions is because I encouraged him to. He told me that it was unclear whether it was the individual employee or the union that was taking this to arbitration. And there had been changes in the way the union has been doing things. And he just didn't know if this contract provision was being honored and satisfied or not. And I said, well, if you don't know, what you can do is ask the executive board whether they support it or not, a simple question and a simple answer. And that's what he did in those two cases. The third claim had to do with Assistant Chief Unfred, who is the liaison to the unions and the police department. He requested a one week extension to complete some shift bidding. And Jeremy Valley as president responded no to the request for an extension and then told him that in dealing with the union, you are to email and communicate only with me, not the other members of the executive board. And Assistant Chief Unfred responded basically, no, I'm gonna continue communicating with everyone on the executive board as I have in the past. So that's the third claim. And the fourth claim has to do with one of the police officers was promoted to detective after a civil service process. And Jeremy Valley was considering grieving that promotion and attempting to take it away. He ultimately decided not to file a grievance. And after he let the deadline for the grievance pass, Assistant Chief Unfred told the officer now, who's now a detective that the deadline had passed and his promotion was now safe. So these are the four issues that were dealt with in this unfair labor practice complaint. We went to hearing in mid 2021, which is two years after the complaint was filed. And there are a couple of reasons for that two year delay. The first one was COVID and the union's attorney initially refused to do a Zoom virtual hearing. And it was many months before PERC could convince him to go to hearing in a virtual format. The first time it was scheduled, the union's attorney called in sick on the day before, on the night before, and that was accepted. And then we had to reschedule for months later.
